\chapter{Counting One to Ten}
\label{ch:ka-numbers-one-to-ten}
\hlchaptermodality{7}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count from one to ten in Kannada, one word at a time, and read each number word off the page in Kannada letters.}

Count ondu through hattu aloud, reading each word in Kannada script, and hear the p to h shift that turns Tamil pattu into Kannada hattu.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ondu]{\kn{ಒಂದು} — one, and the nasal that borrows its sound}

\label{lesson:KA-C07-ondu}



\begin{quote}
Six chapters of letters have gone by. Every shape in the word below is one you have already met, so this is the first word you read rather than recognise.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಒಂದು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಒಂದು}} (\emph{ondu}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{one}.\textquotedblright{}

Tamil says \emph{oṉṟu}. Both come down from an older \emph{oṉ-}, and the family resemblance is easy to hear once you know to listen for it.

Telugu will not join in: its \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} is \emph{okaṭi}, from somewhere else entirely. Of the ten numbers you are about to learn, this is the one that wanders.

The small circle \textbf{\kn{ಂ}} sitting on \kn{ಒ} is the \textbf{anusvara} — a nasal with no fixed sound of its own. Here it borrows \emph{n} from the \textbf{\kn{ದ}} that follows.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}ondu\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ಒಂದು} and find the \kn{ದ} you learned as a letter
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}Tamil oṉṟu, Kannada ondu — same word, new coat\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} in Kannada? (\emph{\textbf{Ondu}}.) Which sister language leaves the family here? (\textbf{Telugu} — \emph{okaṭi}.) What sound is the \kn{ಂ} carrying in \kn{ಒಂದು}? (An \emph{n}, borrowed from the \kn{ದ} after it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[eraḍu]{\kn{ಎರಡು} — two, and the softening that runs through Kannada}

\label{lesson:KA-C07-eradu}



\begin{quote}
One was \emph{ondu}. Say it before you meet the next one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಎರಡು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಎರಡು}} (\emph{eraḍu}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{two}.\textquotedblright{}

Tamil says \emph{iraṇṭu}. Hold the two beside each other and one difference does all the work: where Tamil keeps a hard cluster \textbf{ṇṭ}, Kannada wears it down to a single soft \textbf{ḍ}.

That softening is not a one-off for \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{}. It is a habit of the language, and you will hear it again at \emph{aidu} — \textquotedblleft{}five\textquotedblright{} — in three lessons.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}eraḍu\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ಎರಡು} and find the \kn{ು} that ends it, as it ended \emph{ondu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the count so far — \textquotedblleft{}ondu, eraḍu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count to two. (\emph{Ondu, eraḍu}.) What happened to Tamil's \textbf{ṇṭ} on the way into Kannada? (It softened to a single \textbf{ḍ}.) Which later number will show you the same softening? (\textbf{Five} — \emph{aidu}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mūru]{\kn{ಮೂರು} — three, the number nobody argued about}

\label{lesson:KA-C07-muuru}



\begin{quote}
Two was \emph{eraḍu}, with the softened \textbf{ḍ}. Say it once more.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಮೂರು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಮೂರು}} (\emph{mūru}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{three}.\textquotedblright{}

Tamil \emph{mūṉṟu}, Kannada \emph{mūru}, Telugu \emph{mūḍu}. The endings drift, but the long \textbf{ū} at the front holds firm in all three. Three is the number the family never quarrelled over, and it is a useful anchor: when you meet a Dravidian language you have never studied, look for a word that starts \emph{mū-}.

The long vowel is written with the sign \textbf{\kn{ೂ}} hanging under \kn{ಮ}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}mūru\textquotedblright{} — hold the ū long
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ಮೂರು} and find the long \kn{ೂ} under the first letter
  \item \emph{Say it:} the count so far — \textquotedblleft{}ondu, eraḍu, mūru\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count to three. (\emph{Ondu, eraḍu, mūru}.) What do Tamil, Kannada and Telugu all keep in \textquotedblleft{}three\textquotedblright{}? (The \textbf{long ū} at the front.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ra]{\kn{ರ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S07-letter-ra}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ದ} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ರ}}
\textbf{\kn{ರ}} — \emph{ra}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{r}, it is \textbf{ra}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{ರ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}} \emph{namaskāra} — hello / greetings (namaskāra — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಸರಿ}} \emph{sari} — okay / alright / correct (sari)
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಹೆಸರು}} \emph{hesaru} — name
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನೀವು} \kn{ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ}?} \emph{nīvu hēgiddīrā} — how are you? (respectful)
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ರ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{ರ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{ರ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}  ·  \kn{ಸರಿ}  ·  \kn{ಧನ್ಯವಾದ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ರ} three times, saying \emph{ra} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{ರ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ರ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ra}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nālku]{\kn{ನಾಲ್ಕು} — four, held together by a mark you know}

\label{lesson:KA-C07-naalku}



\begin{quote}
Three was \emph{mūru}. And the small slanting mark \textbf{\kn{್}} — what did it do to the letter under it?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ನಾಲ್ಕು}}
\textbf{\kn{ನಾಲ್ಕು}} (\emph{nālku}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{four}.\textquotedblright{}

Tamil says \emph{nāṉku}. Kannada turned that middle \textbf{ṉ} into an \textbf{l}, and left everything else alone.

Read the word slowly: \textbf{\kn{ನಾ}} (\emph{nā}) · \textbf{\kn{ಲ್}} (\emph{l}, with your virama stripping the vowel away) · \textbf{\kn{ಕು}} (\emph{ku}). Four is where the virama earns its keep — it is what lets \emph{l} and \emph{k} sit together with no vowel between them.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}nālku\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ನಾಲ್ಕು} and find the \kn{್} that joins \kn{ಲ} to \kn{ಕ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the count so far — \textquotedblleft{}ondu, eraḍu, mūru, nālku\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count to four. (\emph{Ondu, eraḍu, mūru, nālku}.) Which Tamil consonant became Kannada's \textbf{l}? (The \textbf{ṉ} of \emph{nāṉku}.) What is the \kn{್} doing inside \kn{ನಾಲ್ಕು}? (Taking the vowel off \kn{ಲ} so it can lean on \kn{ಕ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aidu]{\kn{ಐದು} — five, and a rule you have now seen twice}

\label{lesson:KA-C07-aidu}



\begin{quote}
Two lessons ago Tamil's \textbf{ṇṭ} softened into Kannada's \textbf{ḍ}. Hold that in mind.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಐದು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಐದು}} (\emph{aidu}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{five}.\textquotedblright{}

Tamil says \emph{aintu}. Kannada says \emph{aidu}. The hard \textbf{nt} in the middle has worn down to a soft \textbf{d} — the same wearing-down you met in \emph{iraṇṭu} $\to$ \emph{eraḍu}.

Twice is enough to call it a pattern rather than a coincidence. When a Tamil word you know has a hard cluster in the middle, guess that Kannada softened it, and you will be right more often than not.

\textbf{\kn{ಐ}} is an independent vowel: the shape \emph{ai} takes when it opens a word.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}aidu\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ಐದು} and find the \kn{ದು} that also closes \emph{ondu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the count so far — \textquotedblleft{}ondu, eraḍu, mūru, nālku, aidu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count to five. (\emph{Ondu, eraḍu, mūru, nālku, aidu}.) Which two numbers show the same softening? (\textbf{Two and five} — \emph{iraṇṭu} $\to$ \emph{eraḍu}, \emph{aintu} $\to$ \emph{aidu}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āru]{\kn{ಆರು} — six, and you are halfway}

\label{lesson:KA-C07-aaru}



\begin{quote}
Count from one to five before you add to it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಆರು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಆರು}} (\emph{āru}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{six}.\textquotedblright{}

Tamil says \emph{āṟu}, with a rare trilled \textbf{ṟ} that Tamil keeps and almost nobody else does. Kannada flattened it into an ordinary \textbf{r} — the one you learned as the letter \textbf{\kn{ರ}} a few lessons back.

So the two words are the same word, and the only difference is a consonant Kannada stopped distinguishing.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}āru\textquotedblright{} — long ā, ordinary r
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ಆರು} and find the \kn{ರ} you met as a letter
  \item \emph{Say it:} the count so far — \textquotedblleft{}ondu, eraḍu, mūru, nālku, aidu, āru\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count to six. What did Kannada do with Tamil's rare \textbf{ṟ} in \emph{āṟu}? (Flattened it into an ordinary \textbf{r}.)
\end{tcolorbox}

\label{lesson:KA-S116-letter-ka}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಇ} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.

\textbf{\kn{ಕ}} — \emph{ka}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{k}, it is \textbf{ka}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{ಕ} somewhere inside it:

\end{itemize}

Put your pen on \kn{ಕ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. \subsection*{Your turn}

\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}  ·  \kn{ಧನ್ಯವಾದ}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[ēḷu]{\kn{ಏಳು} — seven, and the letter that replaced Tamil's rarest sound}

\label{lesson:KA-C07-eelu}



\begin{quote}
Six was \emph{āru}. And the letter \textbf{\kn{ಳ}} — say the sound it carries.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಏಳು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಏಳು}} (\emph{ēḷu}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{seven}.\textquotedblright{}

Tamil's word is \emph{ēḻu}, and that \textbf{ḻ} is the sound Tamil is famous for: a curled, almost swallowed sound with no equivalent in most languages.

Kannada let it go. Where Tamil curls, Kannada uses the plain retroflex \textbf{ḷ} — which is exactly the letter \textbf{\kn{ಳ}} you have already been reading.

That trade happened across the whole vocabulary, not only in \textquotedblleft{}seven\textquotedblright{}. A Tamil word with \textbf{ḻ} will usually turn up in Kannada with \textbf{\kn{ಳ}}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}ēḷu\textquotedblright{} — tongue curled back for the ḷ
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ಏಳು} and find the \kn{ಳ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the count so far — \textquotedblleft{}…aidu, āru, ēḷu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}seven\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{ēḷu}.) Which Tamil sound did Kannada give up here, and what took its place? (Tamil's \textbf{ḻ}, replaced by the ordinary retroflex \textbf{ḷ}, written \textbf{\kn{ಳ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[eṇṭu]{\kn{ಎಂಟು} — eight, and the loose end of the family}

\label{lesson:KA-C07-entu}



\begin{quote}
Seven was \emph{ēḷu}, with the letter \kn{ಳ}. Say one to seven.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಎಂಟು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಎಂಟು}} (\emph{eṇṭu}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{eight}.\textquotedblright{}

Kannada \emph{eṇṭu} and Tamil \emph{eṭṭu} are still relatives — near enough to guess at. But \textbf{Telugu} walks away here: its \textquotedblleft{}eight\textquotedblright{} is \emph{enimidi}, and its \textquotedblleft{}nine\textquotedblright{} will be \emph{tommidi}. Neither is recognisable from the other two.

So eight and nine are the loose cells. Everywhere else in this chapter, knowing one Dravidian language hands you the next; at eight and nine it stops doing that, and you have to learn each language on its own terms.

Here the anusvara \textbf{\kn{ಂ}} borrows an \emph{ṇ} from the retroflex \textbf{\kn{ಟ}} after it — the same borrowing you saw in \emph{ondu}, taking a different sound.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}eṇṭu\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ಎಂಟು} and find the \kn{ಂ} — the same mark \emph{ondu} carries, a different sound
  \item \emph{Say it:} the count so far — \textquotedblleft{}…āru, ēḷu, eṇṭu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two numbers should you trust least as family cousins? (\textbf{Eight and nine} — Telugu leaves with \emph{enimidi} and \emph{tommidi}.) What nasal is the \kn{ಂ} carrying in \kn{ಎಂಟು}? (An \textbf{ṇ}, taken from the \kn{ಟ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ombattu]{\kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತು} — nine, and the anusvara's third face}

\label{lesson:KA-C07-ombattu}



\begin{quote}
In \emph{ondu} the \kn{ಂ} said \emph{n}. In \emph{eṇṭu} it said \emph{ṇ}. Watch what it does next.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತು}} (\emph{ombattu}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{nine}.\textquotedblright{} Tamil's \emph{oṉpatu} is the same word underneath.

Now the \kn{ಂ} sits in front of \textbf{\kn{ಬ}}, and a nasal made with the lips is what a \emph{b} wants next to it — so it says \emph{m}. One written mark, three sounds so far, each one decided by the letter after it and never by the mark itself.

That is the whole rule, and it holds everywhere in Kannada: read the \kn{ಂ} forwards.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}ombattu\textquotedblright{} — the m comes from the \kn{ಬ}
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತು} and find the \kn{ಂ} — the same mark \emph{ondu} and \emph{eṇṭu} carry
  \item \emph{Say it:} the count so far — \textquotedblleft{}…ēḷu, eṇṭu, ombattu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}nine\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Ombattu}.) Why does the \kn{ಂ} say \emph{m} here and \emph{n} in \emph{ondu}? (It takes the nasal the \textbf{next} letter asks for — \kn{ಬ} wants \emph{m}, \kn{ದ} wants \emph{n}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hattu]{\kn{ಹತ್ತು} — ten, and the p that turned into h}

\label{lesson:KA-C07-hattu}



\begin{quote}
Nine was \emph{ombattu}. One number left, and it carries the change that most makes Kannada sound like Kannada.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಹತ್ತು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಹತ್ತು}} (\emph{hattu}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{ten}.\textquotedblright{} Tamil says \emph{pattu}.

Kannada softened an old word-initial \textbf{p-} into \textbf{h-}, and did it right across the language: \emph{pāl} became \emph{hālu} (\textquotedblleft{}milk\textquotedblright{}), \emph{pal} became \emph{hallu} (\textquotedblleft{}tooth\textquotedblright{}).

Once you know the rule it runs backwards for you. Meet a Kannada word starting \textbf{h-}, take the \emph{h} off, put a \emph{p} on, and you often have its Tamil cousin.

Every letter in \kn{ಹತ್ತು} is one you have learned: \textbf{\kn{ಹ}}, \textbf{\kn{ತ}}, the virama \textbf{\kn{್}}, and \textbf{\kn{ು}}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}hattu\textquotedblright{} — then \textquotedblleft{}pattu\textquotedblright{}, and hear the trade
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ಹತ್ತು} and read it letter by letter
  \item \emph{Say it:} all ten — \textquotedblleft{}ondu, eraḍu, mūru, nālku, aidu, āru, ēḷu, eṇṭu, ombattu, hattu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count from one to ten in Kannada. What regular change turns Tamil \emph{pattu} into Kannada \emph{hattu}? (Word-initial \textbf{p- to h-} — also \emph{pāl} to \emph{hālu}.) Which number wandered off at the start of the chapter, and which two wandered off near the end? (\textbf{One}, then \textbf{eight and nine}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
